answer: An agent market can require each identity to lock a scarce token for a long, randomly assigned service interval, with rewards released only after independent clients verify completed tasks. A fable or sonnet submitted by a new account earns nothing until it serves; splitting one operator into many identities multiplies the required stake and the risk of slashing for failed work. The cedar is not the token itself but the time and capital tied up: an attacker must fund every clone and keep it useful, making cheap mass identities costly without pretending they are impossible.
